prime.problem: The one-hidden-layer MLP lives in one long block of named tensors (W1, bngain, bnmean_running...). Going deeper means editing the init, the forward pass, the parameter list and the inference code by hand, in step, for every layer, and the lecture's diagnostic plots need to see inside every layer.
prime.fits: It repackages everything so far (the Kaiming-scaled Linear, the BatchNorm forward and its running statistics, tanh) as classes shaped like torch.nn. It's the same idea as micrograd's Neuron/Layer/MLP classes, now on tensors. The diagnostic cards that follow depend on it.
expect: a layer as a class with __call__
a net as a list of 17 layers
prime.goal: Write Linear, BatchNorm1d and Tanh yourself, stack them six layers deep, and explain which tensors backprop trains, which are estimated on the side, and why BatchNorm alone needs a mode flag.

attend: Why can the forward pass shrink to for layer in layers: x = layer(x), and what does each class have to promise for that to work?
Why are running_mean and running_var kept out of .parameters(), even though they change every step?
Of the three classes, why is BatchNorm1d the only one that needs a .training flag?
Where does each of the 47,024 parameters live, and why does dropping the Linear biases still leave more parameters than the no-BatchNorm stack?
Why does every layer keep its output in self.out, when the forward pass would work without it?

must: Every layer implements the same contract (__call__, .parameters()) → the net is just a list → the forward pass is one loop and the parameter list is one comprehension → adding a layer means changing one line, not four places

Parameters get gradients from backprop, but the running stats are moving averages updated under no_grad → they must stay out of .parameters() → otherwise the SGD update has no gradient to apply, and the list would hold a tensor that is replaced every step

BatchNorm's output depends on the whole batch → a single example (or a different batch) gives different or undefined statistics → so it needs a .training flag that switches to the running buffers at inference → forget to flip it and sampling one name gives nan logits

BatchNorm follows every Linear → a Linear bias would be subtracted right back out → bias=False, and BN's β does the shifting → 100 biases out, 200 γ/β in per hidden layer → 47,024 parameters instead of 46,497
elevated: Each layer stores self.out → you can call .retain_grad() on it and histogram activations and gradients per layer → this is what the diagnostic plots on the next cards read
The output layer's γ is multiplied by 0.1 at init → the logits start near zero and the model starts out unsure → step-0 loss 3.2870, close to the uniform 3.2958 (the fix-1 idea, moved from W2 to γ)
reference: the BatchNorm1d(dim, eps=1e-5, momentum=0.1) defaults used by the class
shapes: C 27×10, Linear weights (30, 100), (100, 100) ×4, (100, 27); n_hidden is 100 in this deep net
the notebook's gain line is layer.weight *= 1.0 #5/3, so the measured run uses gain 1
real nn.Linear stores weight as (fan_out, fan_in) and uses a uniform init; model.eval() flips the flag on every sub-module

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the 17-layer stack from Xb to the loss, and write under each layer what .parameters() returns and whether it has buffers. Then explain in 3–4 sentences why this class design makes a deep net easy to build and inspect.
checklist: a shared contract: __call__ computes the layer, .parameters() lists what backprop trains
the net is a list, so the forward pass is one loop and the parameters are collected in one line
BatchNorm has parameters γ, β and buffers running mean/var; buffers are updated by a moving average, not by gradients
the .training flag switches BatchNorm between batch stats and running stats
self.out is kept so each layer's activations and gradients can be plotted

retrieve.q: Explain what a layer has to provide so that for layer in layers: x = layer(x) plus [p for l in layers for p in l.parameters()] is all the network code you need.
answer: a __call__ that takes the previous output and returns this layer's output
a .parameters() that returns its trainable tensors, or [] for Tanh
consistent shapes between neighbours: (32, 30) → (32, 100) → ... → (32, 27)

retrieve.q: Walk through one call of BatchNorm1d.__call__ in training mode and then in inference mode: which statistics are used, what is written back, and what is returned?
answer: training: mean and variance over dim 0 of this batch
normalise with sqrt(var + eps), then gamma * xhat + beta, stored in self.out
training only: under no_grad, blend the batch stats into running_mean/running_var with momentum
inference: use the running buffers and write nothing back

retrieve.q: You add BatchNorm after every Linear. What does that cost and save in parameters, and why is the Linear bias dropped rather than kept alongside β?
answer: the bias is wasted: BN subtracts the batch mean, which removes any constant added before it
per hidden layer: −100 biases, +200 γ/β, so net +100; output layer +27
46,497 → 47,024 (+527), in exchange for normalised preactivations at every layer

retrieve.q: You finish training and sample a name without switching any layer to inference mode. What happens, and exactly why?
answer: each forward is a batch of 1
the unbiased variance of one value is undefined, so BN divides by nan
the logits are nan, and torch.multinomial raises an error about nan probabilities

compare.q: micrograd's Neuron/Layer/MLP classes vs these Linear/BatchNorm1d/Tanh classes: what is the same design idea, what is fundamentally different about what one object represents, and what new kind of state appears here that micrograd never needed?
answer: same: each object is callable and exposes .parameters(), so the training loop is generic
micrograd: one Value per scalar and one class per neuron; here one class holds a whole weight matrix and processes a batch at once
new: buffers and a mode flag, because BatchNorm's output depends on the other examples in the batch
micrograd fails by being too slow; these classes fail through wrong-mode bugs

compare.q: That card keeps bnmean_running as a loose tensor updated in the training loop; this card moves it inside BatchNorm1d as a buffer. What does the move buy you, and what new way to fail does it introduce?
answer: the layer owns its own statistics, so the loop no longer changes as layers are added
switching to inference becomes one flag per layer instead of a separate evaluation function
the new failure: forgetting to set training = False, which silently uses batch statistics

compare.q: Here the net is a plain Python list and the forward pass is a hand-written loop. What would a Sequential-style container add, and when does a plain list stop being enough?
answer: a container is itself a layer: it's callable and collects its children's parameters
then you can nest blocks and flip every child's mode in one call
a plain list is fine for a flat stack, but awkward once layers need to be grouped or reused

predict.q: Keep BatchNorm after every Linear but change the hidden gain from 1 to 5/3, or even 3. Does the step-0 loss move from 3.2870? Commit to a guess, then run it.
predict.answer: It doesn't move: gains 1, 5/3 and 3 all give 3.2870 at step 0. BatchNorm divides each Linear's output by its own batch standard deviation, so multiplying the weights by a constant is cancelled exactly (up to ε). Without BatchNorm the same three gains give 3.2988, 3.2962 and 3.2801. The gain still matters for training, though: it changes the size of the updates, which the update:data ratio card shows.

apply.task: Build the version without BatchNorm: Linear layers with bias=True and Tanh, no BatchNorm1d, layers[-1].weight *= 0.1 for the output, and every hidden Linear weight *= 5/3. Count its parameters and print the step-0 loss. Then take your trained BatchNorm stack, leave training = True, and try to sample one name.
apply.done: The no-BN stack has 46,497 parameters and prints a step-0 loss of 3.2962. Sampling in training mode fails with RuntimeError: probability tensor contains either `inf`, `nan` or element < 0, and setting training = False fixes it.
apply.hint: Use the same seed (2147483647) and create the layers in the same order, so g gives the same random draws. The only changes are the bias flag, removing BatchNorm, and where the 0.1 goes.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the parameter count, or whether the gain changes the loss under BatchNorm?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why buffers aren't parameters, or why only BatchNorm needs a mode flag?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: batch-dependent output → needs a mode flag, or mode flag → running buffers?
Could you rebuild the 47,024 count on paper, layer by layer, without looking?
Before the activation-plot card: do you know which attribute you'll read the histograms from?
